Question

The result of increasing the quantity \(x\) by \(400\%\) is \(60\). What is the value of \(x\)?
rationale_html:
Step 1: Write the multiplier before doing anything else. Increasing a quantity by \(p\%\) multiplies it by \(\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\) ΓÇö the original amount is still there, and the increase is added on top. For \(p = 400\): \(1 + \frac{400}{100} = 1 + 4 = 5\). So "increased by 400%" means ├ù5, not ├ù4.

Step 2: Solve. \(5x = 60 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 12\).

Step 3: Check. \(12 \times 5 = 60\). Confirm it reads correctly as a percent increase: the increase itself is \(60 - 12 = 48\), and \(\frac{48}{12} = 4 = 400\%\). The increase is 400% of the original, exactly as stated.

Why the distractors fail:

  • B. 15 ΓÇö the choice actually selected, and the whole point of the question. It comes from reading "400%" as the multiplier itself: \(4x = 60 \Rightarrow x = 15\). But ├ù4 is what "increased by 300%" means, since \(1 + 3 = 4\). Checking would have caught it: \(15 \to 60\) is an increase of \(45\), and \(\frac{45}{15} = 3 = 300\%\).
  • C. 20 ΓÇö treating the phrase as "increased to 300%" or otherwise dividing by 3. Neither matches the wording.
  • D. 240 ΓÇö multiplying instead of dividing (\(60 \times 4\)), i.e. running the operation in the wrong direction. \(60\) is already the result, so \(x\) must be smaller than \(60\); any answer above \(60\) is eliminable on sight.

Takeaway rule: never let a percent go straight into the equation. Write the multiplier on paper first ΓÇö increase by \(p\%\) ΓåÆ \(\times\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\), decrease by \(p\%\) ΓåÆ \(\times\left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)\) ΓÇö then substitute. Percentages above 100 are where this leaks: +100% is ├ù2, +200% is ├ù3, +400% is ├ù5.

Explanation written by Claude.

Step 4 ΓÇö Confirm D. V(x) = 9x(x ΓêÆ 7): height 9, length x, width x ΓêÆ 7. Plug in a test: if x = 10, then width = 3. Volume = 9 ┬╖ 10 ┬╖ 3 = 270. Check: length (10) is 7 more than width (3) Γ£ô. V(10) = 9┬╖10┬╖3 = 270 Γ£ô.

Rule: Always translate 'A is N more than B' as an equation (A = B + N ΓåÆ B = A ΓêÆ N) before substituting. Never read the comparison direction from the English directly into a formula without the intermediate step.

The "While...it is indisputable" structure signals that this fact stands independent of, even alongside, the new scholarship ΓÇö it describes how Ibn Rushd's works actually circulated.

The old assumption that fits this pattern is that Ibn Rushd was seen as unimportant ΓÇö "inconsequential to" ΓÇö other Muslim philosophers, precisely because his works were mostly known in the West rather than reaching them directly. rationale_html:
Step 1: Statement I ΓÇö the median. Both distributions are symmetric about 13, and the added values in B are symmetric too (one at each end). Symmetry about a center means the center is the median. Median A = median B = 13. Statement I is true.

Step 2: Statement II ΓÇö the standard deviation. Standard deviation measures how far values sit from the mean, not how wide the number line is. Both sets span 10ΓÇô16, so the range is identical ΓÇö that identical range is the trap.

Compare the tails: B has two values at distance 3 from the mean (10 and 16) that A does not have. Every other value is shared. Adding values at the extremes while the mean stays put can only push the average squared distance up.

Takeaway rule: never compare standard deviations by eye or by range. Ask one question instead: which set has more values sitting far from the center? More weight in the tails = larger SD, even when the minimum, maximum, and median are all identical.

Step 2: Name the relationship precisely. Sentence 2 does not add a separate point, and it does not draw a consequence. Step 3: Know the word. Increasingly = "to a greater and greater extent as time passes." It is a degree-over-time adverb, and it is the only choice that carries the temporal trend the sentence supplies evidence for. This is the gap here ΓÇö the relationship was readable, but increasingly wasn't held as a distinct category from ADD/COMPARE words.

Step 4: Rule out each wrong choice.

  • A. Similarly ΓÇö the choice actually selected. Signals COMPARISON: sentence 2 would have to describe a second, parallel case resembling something in sentence 1. But sentence 1 offers no separate case to be parallel to; it announces the very shift sentence 2 then describes. Nothing is being compared to anything.

  • C. Furthermore ΓÇö signals ADD. Closer than A, but wrong all the same: an additive word implies a new, independent point stacked on the first. Sentence 2 is not new information alongside the shift; it is the shift, spelled out.
  • D. Increasingly ΓÇö degree escalating over time, matched by the rising publication counts.

Takeaway rule: the 4-way call (ADD / CONTRAST / RESTATE / CONCLUDE) has a fifth exit ΓÇö DEGREE-OVER-TIME. When three choices differ only in tense and one drops the auxiliary entirely, that pattern is the question telling you it is testing sentence boundaries, not tense.

Step 4: Rule out each wrong choice.

But agreement of tense does not fix structure: "this period is remembered ..., its vehicles are highly prized ..." is two complete sentences joined by a comma. Splice.

  • D. were highly prized ΓÇö same splice, and the past tense also clashes with "is remembered," which describes an ongoing reputation.
  • C. highly prized ΓÇö a past-participial phrase modifying "its vehicles." No second finite verb, so the whole thing stays one grammatical sentence: ΓÇªthis period is remembered for its grandeur, its vehicles highly prized by collectors.

Takeaway rule: two-step check on every FSS blank. (1) Locate the sentence's existing finite verb. (2) If one is already there and the blank sits after a comma with a new subject, the blank must be non-finite ΓÇö a participle (-ing / -ed), never a conjugated verb.   • A. "I see, you don't wish to stopΓÇª" ΓÇö about the girl's unwillingness to linger. No work described, no cheerfulness attributed.
  • D. "Wish I could be out tooΓÇª" ΓÇö expresses Amal's own longing and what he would do if free. It reveals his confinement, not his perception of others as carefree.
  • B ΓÇö both halves present, in Amal's own voice.

Takeaway rule: on "which quotation illustrates the claim," rewrite the claim as a two-item checklist before reading the quotes, then run each quote against both boxes. A quote that echoes the claim's nouns while failing a box is the intended decoy ΓÇö every time. Topical proximity is not evidence.

Passage stored in abbreviated form. The wording below is as logged from the original Bluebook question. The choices and the correct answer are original.

Passage

Adam Smith's "invisible hand" metaphor was putatively used to model how individual self-interest produces aggregate social benefit. But as the scholar Gavin Kennedy has shown, Smith deployed the phrase only once, and narrowly, in a discussion of mercantilism. The metaphor attracted almost no attention for well over a century; it was twentieth-century economists who elevated it into a paradigm of their discipline.

Question

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json:
[{"letter":"A","content":"

The metaphor was largely ignored until economists realized that it anticipated their own views.

"},{"letter":"B","content":"

Economists have given the metaphor undue significance, but it remains a useful model of self-interest.

"},{"letter":"C","content":"

The metaphor was widely interpreted as a model of self-interest but was intended as a critique of mercantilism.

"},{"letter":"D","content":"

The metaphor's reputation is due not to its importance within Smith's own work but to later economists who promoted it for their own ends.

"}]
correct_answer: ["D ΓÇö The metaphor's reputation is due not to its importance within Smith's own work but to later economists who promoted it for their own ends"]
rationale_html:
Step 1: Catch the hedge in sentence 1. Putatively means "supposedly, according to what is generally believed" ΓÇö and it always carries the implication that the belief may not hold up. Its presence tells you, before you read another word, that the text is going to question the standard account of the invisible hand rather than endorse it. Skim past putatively and the passage reads like an appreciation. That single word is the question.

Step 2: Track the argument's arc. Common belief (invisible hand = self-interest model) ΓåÆ Kennedy's correction (used once, narrowly, about mercantilism) ΓåÆ neglect for a century ΓåÆ twentieth-century economists elevate it. Conclusion: the metaphor's fame comes from later promoters, not from any prominence in Smith.

Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice.

  • A. Ignored until economists realized it anticipated their views ΓÇö the choice actually selected. It gets the neglect right, then reverses the passage's judgement with one verb: realized. "Realized" grants that there was something genuinely there to discover, which is the very claim putatively was casting doubt on. The passage's account is appropriation, not discovery. Wrong-polarity distractor ΓÇö right facts, wrong stance.
  • B. Undue significance, but still a useful model ΓÇö the first half matches; the second half praises the metaphor's usefulness, an endorsement the text never offers. Half-right is wrong.
  • C. Interpreted as self-interest, intended as mercantilism critique ΓÇö every element appears in the passage, but this states a detail (Kennedy's finding) rather than the main idea. The passage uses that finding as evidence for a larger point about how the reputation was manufactured.
  • D ΓÇö captures the arc and the skeptical stance.

Takeaway rule: hedging vocabulary ΓÇö putatively, ostensibly, supposedly, reportedly, allegedly, is said to ΓÇö is the author's stance marker. Circle it on sight and write "author doubts this" in the margin before reading the choices. Main-idea questions are then decided by polarity first: kill every choice that endorses the belief the author is hedging, and the field usually drops to one.

label: mistake
stem_html:
Passage stored in abbreviated form. The wording below is as logged from the original Bluebook question. The choices and the correct answer are original.

Passage

A student tracked spider populations in two outdoor enclosures over 30 days ΓÇö one containing lizards, one without them. Observing that the spider count in the lizard enclosure fell sharply over the period, the student concluded that the decline was entirely attributable to predation by the lizards.

Question

Which choice best describes data that, if true, would weaken the student's conclusion?
choices_json:
[{"letter":"A","content":"

The spider count was the same in both enclosures on day 1.

"},{"letter":"B","content":"

The spider count also declined substantially by day 30 in the enclosure without lizards.

"},{"letter":"C","content":"

The largest decline in the lizard enclosure occurred between day 1 and day 10.

"},{"letter":"D","content":"

The spider count on day 30 was lower in the lizard enclosure than in the enclosure without lizards.

"}]
correct_answer: ["B ΓÇö The spider count also declined substantially by day 30 in the enclosure without lizards"]
rationale_html:
Step 1: Isolate the claim's mechanism, word for word. Not "lizards affected spiders" but "the decline was entirely attributable to the lizards." That word entirely is the whole target. To weaken it you need only show that some other factor also drove spiders down ΓÇö you do not have to show lizards did nothing.

Step 2: Ask what the control group is for. The no-lizard enclosure exists precisely to isolate the lizard effect. So the question becomes: what would the control have to show for the claim to break? Answer: a decline there too. That is B, and it can be predicted before reading any choice.

Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice.

  • D. Day-30 count lower in the lizard enclosure ΓÇö the choice actually selected. This is the classic reversal trap: it is a true, relevant fact that strengthens the conclusion. Lower with lizards than without is exactly the pattern the student's claim predicts. "Weakens" questions punish reading for relevance instead of for direction ΓÇö a fact can be about the right thing and still push the wrong way.
  • A. Same count on day 1 ΓÇö establishes that the two enclosures started comparable, which makes the comparison more trustworthy. Neutral at best, strengthening in effect.
  • C. Largest decline in days 1ΓÇô10 ΓÇö describes the timing of the decline inside the lizard enclosure. Timing says nothing about cause; lizards could plausibly eat most heavily early. No bearing on the claim.
  • B ΓÇö if spiders crashed without any lizards present, some other factor (weather, food supply, enclosure conditions) is operating, so the decline cannot be entirely attributable to lizards. It directly negates the quantifier the claim rests on.

Takeaway rule: for "weakens the conclusion," run two steps before touching the choices. (1) Underline the claim's quantifier and mechanism ΓÇö entirely, only, because of X. (2) Say what the world would have to look like for that exact word to be false. Then check each choice for direction, not topic: if a choice fits the claim's predicted pattern, it is a strengthener wearing the right costume.

Some economic historians ______ that late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century households in the United States experienced an economy of scale when it came to food purchases—they assumed that large households spent less on food per person than did small households. Economist Trevon Logan showed, however, that a close look at the available data disproves this supposition.

1. The sentence defines itself twice. The dash restates the blank: “they assumed that large households spent less…” and the final sentence calls it “this supposition.”

2. Match. Surmise = form an idea on little evidence = assumed / supposition.

3. Kill C without vocabulary. If the historians had questioned the idea, Logan disproving it would not be a “however.” The contrast only works if they believed it.

4. Others. Contrived = brought about by trickery. Regretted = felt sorry — no feelings are described, only a belief.

Allen (Aug 16): “Didn't know what vocab meant. Forgot to use context and known vocab to eliminate.” Two tools were available and neither was used: restatement, and logical elimination off however.

Adapted from Jack London's 1903 novel The Call of the Wild. Buck is a sled dog living with John Thornton in Yukon, Canada.

Thornton alone held [Buck]. The rest of mankind was as nothing. Chance travellers might praise or pet him; but he was cold under it all, and from a too demonstrative man he would get up and walk away. When Thornton's partners, Hans and Pete, arrived on the long-expected raft, Buck refused to notice them till he learned they were close to Thornton; after that he tolerated them in a passive sort of way, accepting favors from them as though he favored them by accepting.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

rationale_html:
1. The organising sentence. “Thornton alone held him. The rest of mankind was as nothing.” Every later detail is measured against Thornton — even Hans and Pete are tolerated only once Buck learns they are close to Thornton.

2. Why A fails. A says Buck became less social since he began living with Thornton — a claim about change over time, which needs a picture of Buck before Thornton. The text never gives one. Its comparison is Thornton vs. everyone else, not past-Buck vs. present-Buck.

Allen (Aug 16): “I thought 'the rest of mankind was as nothing' meant he didn't associate with people, therefore being less social.” The clause reading was fine; the failure was not testing the whole choice. Since / has become / more / because smuggle in a second claim the passage must independently support.

A model created by biologist Luis Valente predicts that the rate of speciation—the rate at which new species form—on an isolated island located approximately 5,000 kilometers from the nearest mainland ______ triple the rate of speciation on an island only 500 kilometers from the mainland.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rationale_html:
1. Strip the interrupters. “…predicts that the rate of speciation ______ triple the rate…” That opens a clause; every clause needs a subject and a finite verb. Subject = “the rate of speciation.” The blank is its verb.

2. Sort by finiteness — this is the whole question. being (participle) ✗ · to be (infinitive) ✗ · to have been (perfect infinitive) ✗ · will be (carries future tense) ✓. Three choices die on form alone, before any meaning analysis.

3. Meaning confirms it. The main verb is predicts, so the content of the prediction is future.

Allen (Aug 16): “Should have used context clues — predicts = something in the future.” Right instinct; the faster route is structural — find the clause, ask whether it already has a finite verb. Same rule as PT10 M2 Q17 (‘highly prized’), opposite direction: there the clause already had one, so you needed a participle.

label: PT4
stem_html:
New and interesting research conducted by Suleiman A. Al-Sweedan and Moath Alhaj is inspired by their observation that though there have been many studies of the effect of high altitude on blood chemistry, there is a ______ studies of the effect on blood chemistry of living in locations below sea level, such as the California towns of Salton City and Seeley.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rationale_html:
1. Two words do all the work: though and many. “Though there have been many studies of [high altitude], there is a ___ studies of [below sea level].” Though signals contrast, and what is contrasted is quantity. So the blank must mean few / lack of.

2. Predict, then match. Write “a lack of studies” before reading the choices. Paucity of = scarcity. Match.

3. Why the others die. Profusion of = great abundance — the reverse, killing the contrast (this is the trap for someone who feels the contrast but flips it). Quarrel about = open disagreement — wrong axis; the contrast is amount, not agreement. Verisimilitude in = appearance of truth — also the wrong axis.

Allen (Aug 16): “Didn't know any vocab besides quarrel. Didn't grasp main idea of the text correctly.” Knowing only quarrel is enough to kill A; then ask of each survivor “does this describe how many?” Vocab bank: paucity, profusion, verisimilitude.

label: PT4
stem_html:
Whether the reign of a French monarch such as Hugh Capet or Henry I was historically consequential or relatively uneventful, its trajectory was shaped by questions of legitimacy and therefore cannot be understood without a corollary understanding of the factors that allowed the monarch to ______ his right to hold the throne.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rationale_html:
1. Read the frame, not the topic. “the factors that allowed the monarch to ___ his right to hold the throne.” The blank is a verb taking his claim as its object, and it is something enabling factors let him do. Enabling factors help — so the blank means defend / shore up / strengthen.

2. Match. Buttress = prop up or strengthen. Literal image: the stone buttress holding up a cathedral wall. The monarch's claim is the wall.

3. Why A is the trap. The passage does say legitimacy was questioned — but the blank is about the monarch's response, not the challengers. Disengage = withdraw / detach, i.e. give up the claim, the opposite of what “allowed” implies.

4. B and D. Annotate = add notes — you don't annotate a right. Reciprocate = return a gesture in kind — there is no gesture to return.

Allen (Aug 16): “I thought the passage was talking about their right to hold the throne and people questioning them. Buttress — didn't know meaning.” When the word is unknown, work the grammar frame: subject, object, and whether the surrounding verb implies help or harm. Vocab bank: buttress, reciprocate.

label: PT4
stem_html:
In her poetry collection Thomas and Beulah, Rita Dove interweaves the titular characters' personal stories with broader historical narratives. She places Thomas's journey from the American South to the Midwest in the early 1900s within the larger context of the Great Migration. ______ Dove sets events from Beulah's personal life against the backdrop of the US Civil Rights Movement.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale_html:
1. Map the three sentences — this is claim + two examples. S1 (claim): Dove interweaves personal stories with broader history. S2 (example 1): Thomas → Great Migration. S3 (example 2): Beulah → Civil Rights Movement. S2 and S3 are siblings: both children of S1, neither a child of the other.

2. The one-question test. Does S3 narrow S2 or match it? Different person, different event, same treatment → parallel → COMPARE → Similarly.

3. Why ‘Specifically’ fails. It requires S3 to be a narrower instance of S2 — i.e. Beulah's story an example of Thomas's journey, which is incoherent. Two things both related to a third are parallel to each other, not nested.

4. B and C. Thus = cause→effect; Regardless = concession, but the sentences agree.

Allen (Aug 16): “Didn't read the text close enough and thought the two events were related.” Label each sentence's role (claim / example / consequence / concession) before looking at a single transition word. Same role = COMPARE. On PT10 you knew the relationship but not the word; here the reverse. Do both steps every time.

The minimum value of x is 12 less than 6 times another number n.

Which inequality shows the possible values of x?
rationale_html:
1. Two independent translations. The choices differ on exactly two axes — direction (≤ vs ≥) and expression (6n − 12 vs 12 − 6n). Settle each and the answer is forced.

Axis 1 — direction. A minimum is a floor: x equals it or sits above it. So x ≥ M. (Mirror: maximum is a ceiling → x ≤ M.) Kills A and C.

Axis 2 — expression. “12 less than 6n” → start at 6n, go down 12 → 6n − 12. English puts the subtracted amount first; the arithmetic does not. Kills C and D.

Result: B.

2. Ten-second sanity check. Let n = 3, so 6n − 12 = 6. “The minimum value of x is 6” → x = 6, 7, 100 fine; x = 5 not. x ≥ 6 ✓.

Allen (Aug 16): “Minimum value means x can be greater or equal.” A single inverted symbol on a question you fully understood. Plug in one easy number on any word-to-inequality translation — it catches both a flipped sign and a reversed subtraction.

What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of the resulting graph?
rationale_html:
1. Translate down 4. Shifting down by k replaces y with (y + k):
9x − 10(y + 4) = 19 → 9x − 10y − 40 = 19 → 9x − 10y = 59

4. Keep three things separate. growth factor b = 1.04 · percent of previous = 100b = 104% · percent increase = 100(b − 1) = 4% ← what the question asks. Decay works the same: b = 0.85 → 85% of previous → a 15% decrease.

5. Monic shortcut worth memorising. For x² + bx + c, D < 0 becomes c > b²/4. Here 34²/4 = 289. One line. Geometrically: the parabola's vertex sits above the x-axis, so it never crosses.

57x² + (57b + a)x + ab = 0

In the given equation, a and b are positive constants. The product of the solutions to the given equation is k·ab, where k is a constant.

rationale_html:

product = ab/57 = (1/57)·ab ⇒ k = 1/57
No factoring, no quadratic formula — about fifteen seconds.

2. Factoring route, for confirmation. 57x² + 57bx + ax + ab = 57x(x + b) + a(x + b) = (x + b)(57x + a), so the solutions are −b and −a/57 and their product is ab/57 ✓. The coefficient was written as (57b + a) precisely to signal grouping.

3. On the guess. You wrote 1/57 and swapped to 57 at the last moment. 57 is what you get by inverting the ratio (a/c instead of c/a), and it is the most visually prominent number in the equation — which is why it is offered. Your first instinct was right.

4. Five-second sanity check. Set a = b = 1: 57x² + 58x + 1 = (x + 1)(57x + 1), solutions −1 and −1/57, product 1/57. With ab = 1, k = 1/57 ✓.

Allen (Aug 16): “I guessed. Too lazy to solve. Swapped to 57 instead of 1/57 last minute.” Two fixes, cheapest first: (1) sum/product of solutions → Vieta (−b/a and c/a); (2) with symbolic constants, substitute a = b = 1 and test. Either one removes the coin flip.

An equilateral triangle has perimeter 624 cm. Its height is kΓêÜ3 cm, where k is a constant.

What is the value of k?
rationale_html:
Splitting the equilateral triangle down its height creates two 30-60-90 right triangles, where the height (kΓêÜ3) is the long leg. In a 30-60-90 triangle, if the short leg is k, the long leg is kΓêÜ3, and the HYPOTENUSE (a side of the equilateral triangle) is 2k. So each side of the equilateral triangle = 2k, and perimeter = 3 ├ù (2k) = 6k = 624, giving k = 104. Dividing 624 by 3 directly (624 / 3 = 208) skips the factor of 2 relating k to the actual side length.

Allen's own read: "silly mistake," and the numbers back that up ΓÇö 208 is exactly double the correct answer, meaning the 30-60-90 relationship (side = 2k, not k) got dropped mid-solve rather than a conceptual gap in triangle properties overall.

stem_html:
Two histograms, same shape/frequencies (23 integers each), but Data Set A's bins run 20-60 and Data Set B's identical-shaped bins run 10-50 (each bin shifted down by exactly 10 from A).

What is the smallest possible difference between the mean of Data Set A and the mean of Data Set B?
rationale_html:
Because every bin in B is exactly 10 lower than the matching bin in A, at first glance the means look like they must differ by 10. But integers are only known to fall somewhere WITHIN each bin, not at a fixed point ΓÇö so the smallest gap occurs by pushing Set A's mean to its minimum (values near the bottom of each bin) and Set B's mean to its maximum (values near the top of each bin), which narrows the 10-point bin offset down to just 1.

10 is the tempting "obvious" answer since every bin is offset by exactly 10 ΓÇö the trap is not realizing the individual values inside each bin are still free to vary, which is what lets the two means squeeze closer than the bin offset suggests.
